value.misconception: A framework is just a library.
value.correction: The article emphasizes framework-controlled flow and hooks as inversion of control.

value.misconception: MVC and three-tier architecture are the same.
value.correction: MVC separates software responsibilities; three-tier separates client, application and database.

value.misconception: Frameworks only work for dynamic sites.
value.correction: The article says frameworks can also apply to static sites.

value.misconception: All frameworks render only on the server.
value.correction: The article distinguishes server-side and client-side approaches and says mixed approaches are common.

value.misconception: An SPA is a framework.
value.correction: An SPA is an application architecture that often uses a client-side framework.

value.misconception: HTTP automatically maintains session state.
value.correction: The article describes HTTP as stateless and session management as a separate framework capability.

value.misconception: A cache always serves the request.
value.correction: Cached copies satisfy requests only when cache conditions are met.

value.misconception: Authentication and authorization are identical.
value.correction: Authentication verifies identity; authorization controls access.

value.misconception: ORM and unified DB API are interchangeable.
value.correction: ORM maps objects to records; unified API abstracts database backends.

value.misconception: All routing uses regular expressions.
value.correction: The article describes pattern matching, rewriting and graph traversal.

value.misconception: Ajax requires a full page reload.
value.correction: Ajax exchanges data in the background and updates page regions.

value.misconception: Frameworks always improve runtime performance.
value.correction: Abstractions can add overhead, bundle size and complexity; outcomes depend on context.

value.misconception: Modern standards make all frameworks unnecessary.
value.correction: The article says frameworks remain useful for productivity, structure and edge cases.

value.misconception: Every frontend framework uses a virtual DOM.
value.correction: Svelte is described as compiling components and eliminating the virtual DOM.

value.misconception: Fresh zero-runtime-overhead is an independently verified benchmark.
value.correction: It is a source characterization, not a measurement verified here.

value.misconception: A framework guarantees security.
value.correction: Some provide authentication and authorization; the article does not claim all are secure by default.

value.misconception: The citation warning proves every claim is false.
value.correction: The notice asks for more citations; each claim requires individual assessment.

value.title: Wi-Fi and IEEE 802.11 — Combined Semantic Knowledge Graph
value.purpose: Combined entry that clarifies the relationship between Wi-Fi and IEEE 802.11 while preserving details from both supplied Simple English Wikipedia extracts.
value.scope: Rich semantic graph with directional relationships, mechanisms, conditions, source claims, historical context, models, learning paths, distinctions, questions, misconceptions, and expansion targets.
value.source_policy: The supplied extracts are authoritative for source-derived claims. No external research was performed. Explanatory synthesis is marked as such.
value.provenance_note: The pasted extract has no stable line numbering; provenance is recorded by article and section rather than inventing line ranges.

source_articles.title: Wi-Fi
source_articles.date_note: Includes historical statements framed as of 2007 and 2013.

value.license_note: The supplied Wi-Fi page footer states CC BY-SA 4.0 and mentions GFDL.

value.relationship_semantics: Relationships are directional and typed; causal/explanatory links include mechanism, conditions, and effect where appropriate.

value.name: Typical Wi-Fi-to-Internet path
value.description: A station sends wireless traffic to an access point; a router/gateway forwards traffic to an upstream Internet connection. Devices may combine AP and router roles.

value.name: Radio performance factors
value.description: Band/channel choice, received signal, interference, contention, supported mode, and overhead jointly influence practical performance; no universal deterministic formula is implied.

value.name: 802.11 link architecture
value.description: PHY handles radio signaling; MAC coordinates shared-medium access; together they support wireless LAN links.

value.name: Band-selection trade-off
value.description: Band selection balances congestion, channel availability, device support, coverage, and regulatory constraints.

value.name: Standards-to-ecosystem relationship
value.description: IEEE develops the technical standard family; Wi-Fi is the common ecosystem term associated with compatible WLAN implementations.

value.name: Interference-to-throughput chain
value.description: Competing transmissions can consume airtime or trigger retries and reduce useful throughput; the effect depends on conditions.

value.difference: Formal standards family versus ecosystem/brand term
value.why_it_matters: Prevents conflating the standard family with the common name for compatible WLAN technology.

value.difference: Local wireless link versus upstream service
value.why_it_matters: Wi-Fi may work while Internet service is unavailable.

value.difference: Broad frequency range versus a specific allocation
value.why_it_matters: A band does not identify a single channel.

value.difference: Nominal link rate versus useful delivered data
value.why_it_matters: Link-rate figures are not guaranteed application speeds.

value.difference: Dated claims versus present-day deployment facts
value.why_it_matters: 2007/2013 statements are not current prevalence measurements.

value.difference: What an article attributes to WHO versus fresh evidence evaluation
value.why_it_matters: Preserves attribution without implying independent verification.

value.name: Wi-Fi fundamentals
value.goal: Understand Wi-Fi, IEEE 802.11, stations, access points, and Internet access.

value.name: From radio to useful data
value.goal: Trace radio signaling and channel use to application throughput.

value.name: Understand interference
value.goal: Explain how shared spectrum and competing transmissions can slow a WLAN.

value.name: Compare frequency bands
value.goal: Understand channel and regulatory trade-offs.

value.name: Read standard names
value.goal: Distinguish the original standard and lettered amendments.

value.name: Diagnose speed
value.goal: Separate nominal rates from real-world throughput.

value.name: Wi-Fi versus Internet
value.goal: Understand local wireless connectivity versus upstream Internet service.

value.name: Assess source claims
value.goal: Retain historical context and attribution instead of treating claims as current or independently verified.

value.misconception: Wi-Fi and IEEE 802.11 are exactly the same kind of thing.
value.correction: IEEE 802.11 is the formal standards family; Wi-Fi is the common ecosystem/brand term.

value.misconception: Wi-Fi automatically means the Internet works.
value.correction: A local Wi-Fi link can work while upstream Internet service is unavailable.

value.misconception: A nominal 54 Mbit/s rate guarantees that application throughput.
value.correction: Overhead, contention, interference, retransmissions, and conditions reduce useful throughput.

value.misconception: 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz are standard versions.
value.correction: They are frequency bands; 802.11a/b/g/n/ac/ad are standard/amendment labels.

value.misconception: Every Wi-Fi device can use every channel worldwide.
value.correction: Bands and channels vary by hardware and regulatory domain.

value.misconception: The article’s 2007/2013 statements describe current prevalence.
value.correction: They are historical snapshots.

value.misconception: Wi-Fi literally stands for Wireless Fidelity.
value.correction: The supplied article describes it as wordplay on hi-fi and says it is not short for Wireless Fidelity.

value.misconception: More networks mean data can never get through.
value.correction: Networks may still communicate, but contention and interference can reduce performance.

value.misconception: An attributed health statement is independent verification.
value.correction: The graph records what the supplied article attributes to WHO and does not independently assess the claim.

value.question: What is Wi-Fi?
value.answer: Wireless networking using radio waves rather than wires.

value.question: What does IEEE 802.11 specify?
value.answer: Protocols and behavior for wireless local-area networking.

value.question: How do Wi-Fi and IEEE 802.11 differ?
value.answer: IEEE 802.11 is the standards family; Wi-Fi is the common ecosystem term.

value.question: Does Wi-Fi guarantee Internet access?
value.answer: No; upstream connectivity is separate.

value.question: Which frequency bands are emphasized in the supplied articles?
value.answer: 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz.

value.question: Why can 2.4 GHz be crowded?
value.answer: Multiple wireless technologies and Wi-Fi networks share the band.

value.question: What is a channel?
value.answer: A specific frequency allocation within a broader band.

value.question: What is transmit power control?
value.answer: Adjusting transmit power to what is needed, where required.

value.question: Why does bit rate differ from throughput?
value.answer: Protocol overhead, contention, interference, and retries reduce useful delivered data.

value.question: What year does the article give for the first 802.11 standard?
What rate does the source give for the original standard?
value.answer: 1–2 Mbit/s.

value.question: Which standards does the source say were widely used in 2007?
What introduction date appears in the Wi-Fi infobox?
value.answer: September 1998.

value.question: Which hardware categories are listed?
value.answer: Personal computers, gaming consoles, televisions, printers, mobile phones, and tablets.

value.question: What is an access point?
value.answer: A device that provides wireless connectivity and connects stations to a network.

value.question: What is a Wi-Fi station?
value.answer: A device with a compatible 802.11 interface participating in a WLAN.

value.question: Why may 5 GHz have less congestion?
value.answer: The source says it is less used overall and has more channels; local conditions vary.

value.question: Why does 5 GHz have additional restrictions?
value.answer: Radio regulations constrain channels and operating conditions.

value.question: What is interference?
value.answer: Unwanted or competing radio energy that reduces communication performance.

value.question: What is medium contention?
value.answer: Competition among devices for transmission opportunities on shared airtime.

value.question: Why is global compatibility conditional?
value.answer: Device capabilities, bands, channels, regulations, and configurations differ.

value.question: What does the source say about the Wi-Fi name?
value.answer: It is wordplay on hi-fi and replaced a longer technical label.

value.question: What health statement does the source report?
value.answer: It attributes to WHO the statement that Wi-Fi is not dangerous; this graph does not independently verify it.

value.question: What is a hotspot?
value.answer: A location or device offering wireless network access.

value.question: Which possible interferers are named?
value.answer: Microwave ovens, Bluetooth devices, and DECT telephones.

value.question: Why are 2007 and 2013 claims historical?
value.answer: They are dated snapshots, not current prevalence measurements.

value.question: What is the difference between a band and a channel?
value.answer: A band is a range; a channel is a specific allocation within it.

value.question: What does the MAC layer do?

formal_models.name: Typical Wi-Fi-to-Internet path
formal_models.description: A station sends wireless traffic to an access point; a router/gateway forwards traffic to an upstream Internet connection. Devices may combine AP and router roles.

formal_models.name: Radio performance factors
formal_models.description: Band/channel choice, received signal, interference, contention, supported mode, and overhead jointly influence practical performance; no universal deterministic formula is implied.

formal_models.name: 802.11 link architecture
formal_models.description: PHY handles radio signaling; MAC coordinates shared-medium access; together they support wireless LAN links.

formal_models.name: Band-selection trade-off
formal_models.description: Band selection balances congestion, channel availability, device support, coverage, and regulatory constraints.

formal_models.name: Standards-to-ecosystem relationship
formal_models.description: IEEE develops the technical standard family; Wi-Fi is the common ecosystem term associated with compatible WLAN implementations.

formal_models.name: Interference-to-throughput chain
formal_models.description: Competing transmissions can consume airtime or trigger retries and reduce useful throughput; the effect depends on conditions.

source_claims.claim: The first IEEE 802.11 standard was made in 1997 and allowed 1–2 Mbit/s.
The article estimates around 40–50% of a nominal 54 Mbit/s rate is usable in real-life situations.

The source states three usable channels in 2.4 GHz and 19 in 5 GHz.
source_claims.qualification: Simplified source claim; actual availability depends on country, channel width, and rules.

Wi-Fi is wordplay on hi-fi and was intended to replace a longer technical label.
The article attributes to WHO the statement that Wi-Fi is not dangerous.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Wi-Fi and IEEE 802.11 are exactly the same kind of thing.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: IEEE 802.11 is the formal standards family; Wi-Fi is the common ecosystem/brand term.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Wi-Fi automatically means the Internet works.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: A local Wi-Fi link can work while upstream Internet service is unavailable.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: A nominal 54 Mbit/s rate guarantees that application throughput.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: Overhead, contention, interference, retransmissions, and conditions reduce useful throughput.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Every Wi-Fi device can use every channel worldwide.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: Bands and channels vary by hardware and regulatory domain.

review_questions.question: What is Wi-Fi?
review_questions.answer: Wireless networking using radio waves rather than wires.

review_questions.question: What does IEEE 802.11 specify?
review_questions.answer: Protocols and behavior for wireless local-area networking.

review_questions.question: How do Wi-Fi and IEEE 802.11 differ?
review_questions.answer: IEEE 802.11 is the standards family; Wi-Fi is the common ecosystem term.

review_questions.question: Does Wi-Fi guarantee Internet access?
review_questions.answer: No; upstream connectivity is separate.

review_questions.question: Which frequency bands are emphasized in the supplied articles?
review_questions.answer: 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz.

review_questions.question: Why can 2.4 GHz be crowded?
review_questions.answer: Multiple wireless technologies and Wi-Fi networks share the band.

review_questions.question: What is a channel?
review_questions.answer: A specific frequency allocation within a broader band.

review_questions.question: What is transmit power control?
review_questions.answer: Adjusting transmit power to what is needed, where required.

review_questions.question: Why does bit rate differ from throughput?
review_questions.answer: Protocol overhead, contention, interference, and retries reduce useful delivered data.

review_questions.question: What year does the article give for the first 802.11 standard?
What rate does the source give for the original standard?
review_questions.answer: 1–2 Mbit/s.

review_questions.question: Which standards does the source say were widely used in 2007?
What introduction date appears in the Wi-Fi infobox?
review_questions.answer: September 1998.

review_questions.question: Which hardware categories are listed?
review_questions.answer: Personal computers, gaming consoles, televisions, printers, mobile phones, and tablets.

review_questions.question: What is an access point?
review_questions.answer: A device that provides wireless connectivity and connects stations to a network.

review_questions.question: What is a Wi-Fi station?
review_questions.answer: A device with a compatible 802.11 interface participating in a WLAN.

review_questions.question: Why may 5 GHz have less congestion?
review_questions.answer: The source says it is less used overall and has more channels; local conditions vary.

review_questions.question: Why does 5 GHz have additional restrictions?
review_questions.answer: Radio regulations constrain channels and operating conditions.

review_questions.question: What is interference?
review_questions.answer: Unwanted or competing radio energy that reduces communication performance.

review_questions.question: What is medium contention?
review_questions.answer: Competition among devices for transmission opportunities on shared airtime.

review_questions.question: Why is global compatibility conditional?
review_questions.answer: Device capabilities, bands, channels, regulations, and configurations differ.

review_questions.question: What does the source say about the Wi-Fi name?
review_questions.answer: It is wordplay on hi-fi and replaced a longer technical label.

review_questions.question: What health statement does the source report?
review_questions.answer: It attributes to WHO the statement that Wi-Fi is not dangerous; this graph does not independently verify it.

review_questions.question: What is a hotspot?
review_questions.answer: A location or device offering wireless network access.

review_questions.question: Which possible interferers are named?
review_questions.answer: Microwave ovens, Bluetooth devices, and DECT telephones.

review_questions.question: Why are 2007 and 2013 claims historical?
review_questions.answer: They are dated snapshots, not current prevalence measurements.

review_questions.question: What is the difference between a band and a channel?
review_questions.answer: A band is a range; a channel is a specific allocation within it.

review_questions.question: What does the MAC layer do?
review_questions.answer: Coordinates access to the shared wireless medium.

review_questions.question: What does the PHY layer do?
review_questions.answer: Handles radio signaling and transmission/reception.

review_questions.question: Why separate source claims from synthesis?
review_questions.answer: To preserve what the article says while making explanatory connections transparent.
